question: How do repeats change a forty-second piece?
intro: A child gallops on a stick horse: accented chords in C major, each bar starting with a quaver rest. Both parts of the piece carry repeat signs, and this performance appears to take them, so every bar is heard twice.

sections.label: A · eight bars, played twice
sections.mNote: repeat apparently taken; eight bars sound twice

sections.label: B · sixteen bars, played twice
sections.mNote: chromatic chords, ff in the second half

cues.title: A quaver rest, then off-beat chords
cues.text: Three beats to the bar, marked mf. Each bar begins with a quaver rest in the right hand. Then come a crotchet chord, a quaver chord and an accented crotchet chord, off the beat against long left-hand notes. The gallop is in that long–short–long figure. The first eight bars close with a repeat sign.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 13 (IMSLP #03060): 3/4, no sharps or flats, mf, quaver rest at the start of each bar, then crotchet, quaver and accented crotchet chords, long left-hand notes, closing repeat sign after bar 8. Report: C major (G C E among the strongest pitch classes at 0:00–0:10), 3.8–4.6 onsets per second.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Both repeats are taken
cues.text: The second part has sixteen bars and its own repeat sign. With both repeats the piece runs 48 bars. The recording lasts 44 seconds including its slowing and decay, about 0.9 seconds a bar, so both repeats appear to be taken, and each pass of the second part lasts about 14 seconds.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 1.00 at 0:14, the only structural boundary. Onset-envelope autocorrelation peaks at 0.267 s and 0.813 s, consistent with a three-beat bar near 0.8–0.9 s. Form analysis: 0:08.5–0:22.5 matches 0:22.5–0:36.5 (lag 14 s, mean 0.95). 44 s over 48 bars is about 0.9 s a bar, allowing for the final slowing; the boundary at 0:14 then falls after 16 bars (the first part with its repeat). Score p. 13: repeat signs after bar 8 and after bar 24.

cues.title: A title on a list, a publisher chased
cues.text: Schumann named this piece in his March 1838 list of titles for Clara. By 6 July he was pressing the publisher Raimund Härtel about the set: “sie werden zu alt mit der Zeit”, they will grow too old with time. The first edition appeared in 1839.
cues.evidence: Zwickau catalogue, item 3 (title list including “Ritter vom Steckenpferd”) and item 6 (letter to Härtel, 6 July 1838); IMSLP lists the first publication as Breitkopf & Härtel, Leipzig, 1839.

transitions.title: The same gallop over new harmony
transitions.how: After the repeat of the first eight bars, the second part keeps the rhythm of the first: a quaver rest, then the long–short–long chords with their accent. What changes is the harmony, with flat and natural signs in the chords, and the dynamic, which reaches ff in the second half of the part. The rhythm stays fixed, so the change comes only from harmony and volume.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 1.00 at 0:14 with level −8.3 dB at 0:10 and −5.6 dB at 0:15. Score p. 13: double bar with repeat signs after bar 8, flat and natural signs in the third system, ff in the fourth.

composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
